items.readme:
Pinky

Let any AI agent use your iPhone or Android phone, from macOS, Windows or Linux, with you in the loop.

Download · Get started · FAQ · Discord

English · 简体中文 · 日本語


A real Claude Code run on an Android 16 emulator. Pinky asks before payments by default; this run also asks before messages.

Pinky lets any agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor or a script) operate a real iPhone or Android phone over MCP, while you watch on your computer, approve risky steps, take over and review what happened. Approvals are enforced by Pinky's gateway, not by instructions to the agent. - **Every platform.** One app for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux. It drives Android phones (Android 10 to 17) and iPhones on iOS 17.4 or later: nothing to install on iOS 27 and later, and a helper installed once from Xcode on iOS 17.4 to 26, which you can also choose on iOS 27 (tried there, on a phone below it and on Simulators; [details](#phones)). - **Tiny and native.** The window is drawn by [MyGo](https://github.com/egoist/mygo) on the GPU, with no Electron and no webview: a 16–22 MB download that idles at about 70 MB of memory and 0% CPU on a Mac. - **Any agent, one click.** Settings › Agents connects Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor and more, and any agent that can use MCP servers works, on the same computer or over HTTP. - **Locked phone? Unlock it from your computer.** Save the phone's PIN in Pinky once, then confirm each unlock with Touch ID, Windows Hello or your keyring's password. Agents never see the PIN. - **Free and open source** under the Apache-2.0 license, with no account to create.

You approve the risky steps. Payments, trades and transfers wait for your click; in Settings › Safety you can have sends, orders, deletions, calls, installs, links that leave the app and settings changes wait too, or every step. Pinky spots these buttons in 10 languages. The rules run in Pinky's gateway, so an agent can't approve itself, even when text on the screen tries to talk it into it.
Off-limits by default. Banking, wallet and password-manager apps are invisible to agents, and agents can't type into password or one-time-code fields. When an agent needs a banking or wallet app for a task, it asks, and you can allow that app for that task only. Every new agent needs your approval and gets only the scope you give it.

Your phone stays yours. On Android 13 and later, agents work on a hidden second screen, so the phone's own screen stays yours, or off and locked. On older Android phones and on iPhones they use the main screen.
Take over any time. Click the mirror and the agent pauses until you hand back; on Android, touching the phone yourself pauses it too. Stop all is ⌥⌘. (Ctrl+Alt+. on Windows and Linux) from anywhere.

Every run is on the record. Each step in plain words, screenshots and a screen recording with a mark per step, exportable as an HTML report. It all stays on your computer.
iPhones too. The same gateway, approvals and records work on iOS 17.4 and later (what works). Shown here on the iOS Simulator, with deletions set to ask.
**Status:** pre-alpha. Claude Code has used real phones through it end to end (an Android phone over USB, an iPhone on iOS 27, and an iPhone XS Max on iOS 18.7.11 through the helper), and agents can connect over stdio or HTTP. Unlocking from the computer, background work on Android, recordings, export, Wi-Fi pairing and the phone's files are built; some of it still waits for a person to try it. See [docs/ACCEPTANCE.md](docs/ACCEPTANCE.md) for what works today and how to try it. ## Get started Install Pinky, connect your phone and add Pinky to your agent. Then ask the agent to do something on the phone, and watch it work in Pinky's window. ### What you need | | You need | | --- | --- | | **Mac** | macOS 13 or later, with Apple silicon or Intel | | **Windows** | Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit (x64) | | **Linux** | A 64-bit PC (x86-64) with Ubuntu 20.04, Debian 11 or a newer system (glibc 2.29 or later), and GTK 3 | | **Android phone** | Android 10 to 17 and a USB cable. Pinky brings its own adb; on Windows some phones need a USB driver, and on Linux USB access ([below](#usb-on-windows-and-linux)) | | **iPhone or iPad** | iOS 17.4 or later, and a USB cable to set it up; afterwards it works over Wi-Fi too ([below](#iphones-and-ipads-over-wi-fi)). Pinky prepares it itself, with Apple's developer disk image, which comes with Xcode or which Pinky can download from a third-party mirror when you ask ([below](#iphone)). On iOS 17.4 to 26 also a helper app on the iPhone ([below](#iphones-on-ios-174-to-26)) | | **Simulators and emulators** | Optional, in place of a phone or next to one: an iOS Simulator on a Mac with Xcode, or an Android emulator from Android Studio. You create them there; Pinky starts them ([below](#phones)) | | **Agent** | Any agent that can use MCP servers, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex or Cursor | ### 1. Download and install Pinky Get Pinky from [the latest release](https://github.com/DIYgod/pinky/releases/latest): - **Mac:** download `pinky--arm64.dmg` for a Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later) or `pinky--amd64.dmg` for an Intel Mac. Open it and drag Pinky to Applications. With [Homebrew](https://brew.sh), `brew install --cask diygod/tap/pinky` does the same. - **Windows:** download `pinky-setup--amd64.exe` and run it. It installs Pinky for your account, without administrator rights. The installer is not signed yet, so SmartScreen may say that Windows protected your PC: choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**. To use Pinky without installing it, unzip `pinky--windows-amd64.zip` and open `Pinky.exe`. - **Linux:** on Debian and Ubuntu, download `pinky__amd64.deb` and install it with `sudo apt install ./pinky__amd64.deb`. On other systems, unpack `pinky--linux-amd64.tar.gz` into a folder of its own and run `pinky` in it. Pinky looks for new versions by itself and, on a Mac, with the Windows installer and unpacked from the Linux `.tar.gz`, installs them too ([Updates](#updates)). ### 2. Connect your phone Open Pinky and choose **Add phone**. A phone that is ready shows up in Pinky's window; when something is missing, the phone's page in Pinky says what. #### Android **Add phone › Android** shows these steps for your phone's brand, with its own menu names and extra switches: Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo, HONOR, HUAWEI, Samsung and Pixel, and general steps for the rest. 1. On the phone, turn on USB debugging: in Settings › About phone, tap **Build number** 7 times, then turn on **USB debugging** in Settings › System › Developer options. Some brands name these menus a little differently. 2. Plug the phone into the computer. When the phone asks whether to allow USB debugging, tap **Allow**. On Android 11 and later you can pair it over Wi-Fi instead, from **Add phone** ([when it fails](#when-pairing-over-wi-fi-fails)). Android 10 has no Wireless debugging: once it is plugged in, **Use Wi-Fi instead…** moves it to Wi-Fi ([below](#phones)). 3. Pinky offers to install Pinky Companion, its app for the phone, which makes reading the screen many times faster and lets Pinky type in any language. The phone may ask you to allow the install once. Each phone has a **Checkup**, in the ··· menu under its mirror, that lists what works and how to fix what doesn't, such as a Xiaomi's USB debugging (Security settings) switch. Over Wi-Fi, Pinky makes sure the phone that answers is yours: it leaves a mark on each phone it sets up, which only the phone's debugging connection can read, and checks it whenever adb connects the phone, so another device on the network can't answer in its place. A phone connected over Wireless debugging that Pinky hasn't used, by another tool for example, shows as found on Wi-Fi, and Pinky leaves it alone until you choose **Use**. If a phone's page says **This may not be …** after you reset the phone or set it up again yourself, choose **Trust this phone…** there, or plug it in once. Taking the phone out? With Tailscale, Pinky reaches it away from home too ([how](#phones-away-from-home)).

Add phone › Android, with a Xiaomi picked.
A Redmi's Checkup, with two things to fix.
#### Android tools Pinky brings its own adb, the tool it reaches Android phones with, built from Android's source, so nothing else needs installing. When the computer has Android's platform tools already, from Android Studio, Homebrew or the system's packages, Pinky uses those, and shares their adb server with Android Studio and other tools. When Pinky quits, it stops the adb it brought, unless another app such as Android Studio is using it; Settings › Advanced › **Stop adb when Pinky quits** turns that off. An adb you installed keeps running. #### USB on Windows and Linux - **Windows:** the phone's USB debugging needs a driver. Windows installs one by itself for many phones; when it has none, Pinky lists the phone as needing setup and says which driver to install: the [Google USB Driver](https://developer.android.com/studio/run/win-usb) for Pixels, [Samsung's](https://developer.samsung.com/android-usb-driver) for Samsung phones, the [phone maker's](https://developer.android.com/studio/run/oem-usb) for others. Unplug the phone and plug it in again afterwards. - **Linux:** the computer must let Pinky open the phone's USB device, which takes udev rules for Android phones: `sudo apt install android-sdk-platform-tools-common` on Debian and Ubuntu, `android-udev` on Arch, `android-tools` on Fedora. You may also need to be in the `plugdev` group. Then plug the phone in again. Pinky says so when they are missing. #### When pairing over Wi-Fi fails When a phone works on the cable but **Pair over Wi-Fi** does not finish, the pairing page says within half a minute what Pinky sees: - **The phone hasn't shown up on the network yet:** check that Wireless debugging is on and that the phone is on the same Wi-Fi as the computer. Guest Wi-Fi, routers with AP (client) isolation and many office networks keep devices from finding each other. There, choose **Pair with a code instead**: on the phone, tap **Pair device with pairing code** and enter the IP address and port and the six-digit code it shows, which change each time that dialog opens. Pinky then needs no search to pair; if it still cannot find the phone afterwards, it asks for the IP address and port at the top of Wireless debugging (not the pairing dialog's) and connects there. If it cannot reach the phone at those addresses either, the network keeps its devices apart: use a Wi-Fi where they can reach each other, such as your home network rather than its guest network, or the cable. - **Pinky isn't allowed to look for phones on this network:** on a Mac, Pinky needs Local Network access, and macOS gives no error without it: the search just finds nothing. Choose **Open Local Network settings**, turn on Pinky under System Settings › Privacy & Security › Local Network and try again (if macOS asks whether Pinky may find devices on your local network, click **Allow**). On a Mac, a phone's **Checkup** shows this too, under **Local network**. On Windows and Linux, a firewall can block the search the same way: let Pinky use the local network, or pair with a code. - **Pinky can't look for phones on this network:** check that the computer is connected to Wi-Fi or Ethernet. - **The phone showed up, but pairing hasn't finished:** if the phone shows an error or went back to Wireless debugging, scan the code again, or pair with a code. When pairing stops with an error, the page says what adb reported: - **The phone ended the pairing before it finished** (QR code): the phone left its scanning screen, changed Wi-Fi, or something between it and the computer cut the connection; adb cannot tell which. Keep the phone on the scanning screen and try again, or choose **Pair with a code instead** next to the message. - **The phone didn't accept the pairing** (pairing code): a wrong code, or a port that is not the pairing dialog's. The address at the top of Wireless debugging is for connecting, not pairing, and adb answers the same way for both mistakes. - **Nothing at that address is waiting to pair** or **The phone stopped waiting to pair:** the pairing dialog or the scanning screen closed, or the port is wrong. Open it again and use what it shows now. - **Couldn't reach the phone at that address** or **Pinky couldn't connect to it:** the network keeps the computer and the phone apart, as above; a VPN or firewall on the computer can too. - **The adb server running on this computer is too old:** another program started an adb older than platform-tools 30. Quit it, or update it, and Pinky starts its own. Pinky writes adb's own words to its log, which **Help › Send Feedback…** attaches with the diagnostics. Pairing over Wi-Fi needs Android 11 or later; an Android 10 phone moves to Wi-Fi from the cable instead (**Use Wi-Fi instead…**, [below](#phones)). Up to Android 16, Wireless debugging turns itself off when the phone leaves the Wi-Fi network, even for another access point of it, or restarts: turn it on again, or pair again from **Add phone**. #### iPhone Pinky prepares an iPhone itself; **Add phone › iPhone** walks you through it. 1. Plug the iPhone into the computer, unlock it, tap **Trust** and enter its passcode. On Windows, install Apple Devices from the Microsoft Store (or iTunes) first; on Linux, the `usbmuxd` package. Add phone says when they are missing. 2. On the iPhone, turn on **Developer Mode** in Settings › Privacy & Security: Pinky makes the switch appear there. The iPhone restarts; unlock it, tap **Turn On** and enter the passcode. 3. Pinky mounts Apple's developer disk image on the iPhone and lists it as ready. An iPhone on iOS 27 keeps the image when it restarts; below iOS 27 Pinky mounts it again after each restart, once you unlock the iPhone. The developer disk image comes with [Xcode](https://apps.apple.com/app/xcode/id497799835), Apple's free app for developers, and Pinky does not ship it. On a Mac, install Xcode once and open it: Pinky uses the image it installs, and Xcode never has to run again. An iPhone on iOS 27 or later needs the image of Xcode 27 or later: Apple's signing server no longer signs older ones, and Add phone then says which image Pinky used and how to get a newer one. On Windows and Linux, copy `/Library/Developer/DeveloperDiskImages/iOS_DDI` from such a Mac into Pinky's folder ([where](docs/notes/ios.md#preparing-a-phone-without-xcode)). Without either, or when Apple refuses the image Pinky found (Xcode's, or one copied into Pinky's folder), Add phone offers to download the image from a third-party mirror, github.com/doronz88/DeveloperDiskImage (Xcode 27.0 beta 4, 32 MB, kept by the author of pymobiledevice3, not by Apple), only when you click Download; Pinky checks every file against the checksum it expects, and from then on uses it instead of an image Apple refused. On iOS 27 and later, no app gets installed on the iPhone. Checked on the iPhone 13 mini (iOS 27.0.1): Pinky mounting Xcode's image itself (in about 1.5 s, after the image had been taken off), keeping the image already on the phone, and that the iPhone keeps the image when it restarts. Not yet tried on a phone: the downloaded image, the Developer Mode switch, iPhones below iOS 27, and pairing an iPhone on Windows. Contributors have used an iPhone and an iPad on iOS 27.2 on Linux (Arch Linux), and an iPhone on iOS 27.2 on Windows 11, on the cable and over Wi-Fi, with the image already on them. #### iPhones and iPads over Wi-Fi Pinky also uses an iPhone or iPad over Wi-Fi while it is on the same Wi-Fi as the computer, and the computer lists it there, which it does once Wi-Fi connections are on for the phone. Pinky turns them on when you plug the phone in and it trusts the computer: it is the same setting as Finder's **Show this iPhone when on Wi-Fi**, so a phone already set up that way stays as it is. It is on by default; **Settings › Phones › Use iPhones and iPads over Wi-Fi** turns it off, which leaves the phones' setting alone. If a phone doesn't show up on Wi-Fi when you unplug it, its **Checkup** says where it stands under **Wi-Fi**: whether its Wi-Fi connection is on and whether Pinky turned it on, why Pinky couldn't, and whether this computer sees the phone on Wi-Fi. - An iPhone or iPad Pinky has used keeps working when you unplug it, as the same phone with its settings: Pinky moves it to Wi-Fi by itself, and back to the cable when you plug it in, and an agent's task goes on; its calls wait a few seconds meanwhile. - One Pinky has not used, such as a family member's iPad paired with this computer, shows as **Found on Wi-Fi**. Pinky reads its name, model and iOS version and does nothing else, and agents don't see it, until you choose **Use**, which sets it up over Wi-Fi, or **Ignore**, which keeps it off the list until you plug it in. - A locked iPhone or iPad on Wi-Fi shows as **Locked on Wi-Fi**, and Pinky connects to it once you unlock it: while it sleeps it drops off the network every minute or so, and connecting to it then lights its screen. - Setting one up over Wi-Fi: trusting the computer needs the cable, and so does making the Developer Mode switch appear while it is hidden (on a phone used with Xcode it shows already). Turning Developer Mode on happens on the phone, and Pinky mounts the developer disk image over Wi-Fi too, in about 9 s instead of 1.5 s. **Add phone › iPhone** says which step needs the cable. - Over Wi-Fi, Pinky talks only to the phone it paired with: it checks the certificate the phone got when it first trusted this computer, so another device on the network can't answer in its place. Below iOS 27, the WebDriverAgent helper's connection isn't encrypted, so there it is only as safe as the Wi-Fi. Over Wi-Fi each step is slower than on the cable, screenshots most of all. Measured on an iPad Pro 11-inch (3rd generation, iPadOS 27.0.1), Wi-Fi against the cable: a swipe shows on screen after 80 to 210 ms (60 to 90 ms), the home screen reads in 0.6 to 2.6 s (0.5 to 0.6 s), a screenshot takes 5 s (1 s), and 0.2 % of the video's packets were lost (none). Unplugging moved a running task to Wi-Fi in about 5 s, and plugging in moved it back in 2 to 6 s ([details](docs/notes/ios.md#wi-fi)). On a Mac, the system's device service, usbmuxd, can lose an iPhone on Wi-Fi after its connection broke once (its Wi-Fi turned off and on, say), and not look for it again for up to about an hour; Finder loses it too. Pinky notices when a phone you use is on the network but no longer listed, shows it as **Lost on Wi-Fi**, and offers **Restart device service…** on its page: after you confirm, macOS asks for an administrator's password, and every iPhone and iPad, also on a cable, disconnects for a second or two. `sudo killall usbmuxd` in Terminal does the same. Right after you unplug a phone it says so within about 10 seconds; it waits a minute otherwise, as a phone that wakes comes back by itself. A phone you unplug that this computer doesn't see on Wi-Fi at all shows as **Not seen on Wi-Fi**, with what may hide it: it's asleep, on another network or one that keeps devices apart (guest networks, some routers), a VPN, or Pinky not allowed on the local network. On Linux and Windows, the system's device service does not list iPhones and iPads on Wi-Fi by itself: on Linux (the `usbmuxd` package) it lists them only on the cable, and on Windows (Apple Devices or iTunes) only while they are on the cable too. So there Pinky runs a small device service of its own in front of the system's, while it uses phones over Wi-Fi: it finds the phones paired with this computer on the network and connects to them directly, and passes everything about phones on a cable to the system's. All of Pinky's connections to iPhones and iPads go through it then, on the cable too. There is nothing to install or set up for it beyond the system's own (`usbmuxd` on Linux, Apple Devices on Windows). If you run a device service that lists phones on Wi-Fi itself, such as netmuxd, and start Pinky with `USBMUXD_SOCKET_ADDRESS` pointing at it (`unix:///path/to/socket` or `tcp://127.0.0.1:port`), Pinky uses that one instead and runs none of its own. While Pinky opens a phone, or moves it between the cable and Wi-Fi, it shows **Connecting** or **Moving to Wi-Fi** rather than offline. Over Wi-Fi Pinky reads text from the live picture rather than from screenshots, which take about 5 s there. An iPhone or iPad without a passcode never reads as locked, so after it has dropped off the network to sleep, Pinky connects to it only once it has been back for 30 seconds. #### iPhones on iOS 17.4 to 26 Below iOS 27, an iPhone takes taps and typing from a computer only through a helper app on the phone: WebDriverAgent, which you build and install once from Xcode with your Apple ID ([how](docs/notes/ios.md#installing-the-webdriveragent-helper)). With a free Apple ID it has to be installed again every 7 days: two days before, the phone's page and its checkup remind you, and once it has run out the phone shows as needing setup and says why ([how to install it again](docs/notes/ios.md#when-the-helpers-signature-runs-out)). It has been tried on an iPhone XS Max on iOS 18.7.11, on Windows, over its cable and Wi-Fi. Without it, Pinky can only show and read the screen (on a Mac) and open apps: no taps, swipes or typing. iOS 17.3 and earlier are not supported. ### 3. Add Pinky to your agent In Pinky, open **Settings › Agents** and click **Connect** next to your agent. Pinky finds Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Copilot CLI, Windsurf (Devin Desktop) and Gemini CLI on your computer and adds itself to the agent's MCP servers, by the app's own path: with the agent's own command where it has one, such as `claude mcp add`, or in its settings file, which Pinky copies first and changes only in Pinky's entry. It also installs Pinky's agent guide, [SKILL.md](docs/SKILL.md), where the agent reads skills, and keeps it current: when Pinky updates, it rewrites the guide it installed to the new version's. Until an agent is connected, a card in Pinky's sidebar offers to do it, or says where to get one.

- **Claude Desktop:** Connect opens Pinky's extension in Claude Desktop; click **Install** there. Add an MCP server (stdio) that runs it. In a JSON config, with the Homebrew cask or a Linux package: ```json { "mcpServers": { "pinky": { "command": "pinkyctl", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` Claude Code in a terminal: `claude mcp add --scope user pinky -- pinkyctl mcp`. Most agents read the guide from `~/.agents/skills/pinky/SKILL.md`, Claude Code from `~/.claude/skills/pinky/SKILL.md`. The command is `pinkyctl`, not `pinky`: many computers already have another program named `pinky`. An agent on another computer or in a container can connect over HTTP instead ([how](docs/mcp.md#over-http)). [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md#connecting-an-agent) says what Connect changes for each agent. ### 4. Screens, typed text, app names, phone names and ids, PINs and file names are never sent. Help › Send Feedback… opens a GitHub issue with your message and diagnostics filled in, which you read and submit yourself. [docs/TELEMETRY.md](docs/TELEMETRY.md) lists everything. ## FAQ
Which agents work with Pinky? Any agent that can use MCP servers: over stdio, by running `pinkyctl mcp`, or over HTTP with an agent token ([how](docs/mcp.md#over-http)). **Settings › Agents** connects Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor and other agents it finds on your computer in one click. Claude Code is the one that has used real phones end to end so far. Pinky brings no model of its own: your agent does the thinking.
Where does Pinky keep its files, and can I move them? Pinky keeps its settings, history and the socket agents reach it through in your user folders: `~/Library/Application Support/Pinky` on a Mac; `%APPDATA%\Pinky` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Pinky` on Windows; `~/.config/pinky`, `~/.local/share/pinky` and `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/pinky` on Linux. To keep all of them in one folder of your choice instead, set the environment variable `PINKY_HOME` to it: Pinky then uses `config`, `data` and `run` inside it. Set it where both Pinky and your agents see it, such as a user environment variable on Windows, or also in the agent's MCP settings (`"env": { "PINKY_HOME": "…" }`): a Pinky started without it uses the usual folders and doesn't see the other. On macOS and Linux the socket's path has to stay short, about 100 characters, and Pinky says so when `PINKY_HOME` makes it too long. On Windows, agents reach Pinky through a named pipe, which works from packaged (MSIX) apps such as the Claude and Codex desktop apps too. Older versions of Pinky listened on a socket file in AppData, which those apps can't see; update Pinky if an agent in one of them can't reach it.
Can an agent approve its own risky step, or be talked into it? No. The rules run in Pinky's gateway, between the agent and the phone. A step that needs you comes back to the agent as `approval_pending`, and nothing happens on the phone until you click **Allow** in Pinky; the agent has nothing it could send to confirm it. Before acting, Pinky checks that the button is still where it was, and no answer within 60 seconds means no. Pinky finds these buttons by their labels in 10 languages, so an unusual one could slip through: for more control, Settings › Safety has **Ask before every action** and **Read-only mode**.
What can't agents see? Banking, wallet and password-manager apps, from a list that comes with Pinky and that you can add to in Settings › Safety, where you pick the app from those on your phones: agents get no screen from them, and their notifications are hidden, in the notification shade and on the lock screen too. Where another screen shows a blocked app, as its notification in the shade or in a banner, or its card in recent apps, the agent reads only that something is hidden there, and the screenshots it gets, and those in Activity, cover it with a gray box (screen recordings show it as it was, so they stay on your computer: an agent gets one only when you allow it at an export). Agents can't type into password or one-time-code fields. When an agent needs a banking or wallet app for a task, Pinky asks you first. If you allow it, the agent may open and read that app for the rest of the task, what your rules ask about there still asks, and Pinky keeps no screenshots or recordings of it: to read text that only its pixels show, Pinky looks at its screen in memory and gives the agent the text, never the picture. Password managers are never offered. One-time codes are masked before an agent reads them: in a text message, an email, a notification or anywhere else on the screen, "Your code is 482913" reaches the agent as "Your code is ••••••", and the screenshots it gets, and those in Activity, have the code covered with a gray box. Prices, phone numbers, dates and numbers in text that is not about a code stay as they are. Screen recordings show codes as they were, so they stay on your computer: an agent gets one only when you allow it, each time it exports a task's report. You can turn this off in Settings › Safety › Hide codes from agents.
Does my phone's screen go to the cloud? Not through Pinky. Screenshots, recordings and history stay on your computer, for 30 days unless you change it in Settings › Privacy, where you can also delete them. What the agent reads, the screenshots and reports it saves, and a screen recording when you allow it at an export go to the agent you chose, as with any tool you give it. Pinky's anonymous usage statistics never include screens, typed text or app names ([above](#usage-statistics-crash-reports-and-feedback)).
What does Pinky install on my phone? On Android, Pinky Companion, when you click Install; Pinky keeps it up to date and turns its accessibility service on only while an agent works ([why](#faq)). On an iPhone, no app on iOS 27 and later: Pinky mounts Apple's developer disk image, as Xcode does. On iOS 17.4 to 26, the WebDriverAgent helper, which you install once from Xcode ([how](docs/notes/ios.md#installing-the-webdriveragent-helper)).
How do I install Pinky Companion by hand? When a phone won't let the computer install apps over USB, such as a Xiaomi without a SIM card, which can't turn on Install via USB, you can install Pinky Companion yourself. Its APK, `pinky-companion.apk`, comes with Pinky: - **macOS:** inside the app, at `Pinky.app/Contents/Resources/pinky-companion.apk`: in Applications, right-click Pinky and choose **Show Package Contents**. - **Windows:** next to `Pinky.exe` in Pinky's folder. - **Linux:** next to `pinky` in the folder you unpacked the `.tar.gz` into, or in `/opt/pinky/` if you installed the `.deb`. When an install over USB fails, **Show pinky-companion.apk** on the phone's page shows you the file. Copy it to the phone, over the cable or through a chat app for example, and open it there; the phone may ask you first to let the app you open it with install apps. Pinky recognizes the copy you installed, as it is the same app with the same signature, and stops offering to install it. On a Xiaomi, Redmi or POCO phone, Pinky still needs **USB debugging (Security settings)** in Developer options to tap and type, and to turn on Pinky Companion's accessibility service; restart the phone after you turn it on. Like Install via USB, that switch checks with Xiaomi online and may ask for a SIM card. Without it, Pinky Companion installs but can't come on, and Pinky can't tap or type on the phone. Pinky Companion gets a new version only when its own code changes, not with every Pinky update. With **Update automatically** on, Pinky tries once to install a new version over USB; when the phone refuses, a card in the sidebar tells you, with **Show pinky-companion.apk**, and Pinky doesn't try that version again. Install the new `pinky-companion.apk` the same way. With **Update automatically** off, the phone's page offers the new version when you open it.
Will banking or other apps notice Pinky Companion? While its accessibility service is on, they can. Malware abuses accessibility services, so many banking apps refuse to sign in while an app from outside an app store has one turned on: in Malaysia (Maybank, CIMB, HSBC and the other members of the Association of Banks in Malaysia, since 2024) and in Singapore (DBS, OCBC and UOB, since 2023) among others. Pinky Companion is such an app, as Pinky installs it over USB. Apps such as WeChat, Douyin and Xiaohongshu can see the service too and watch for automated use; we know of no report that they flagged Pinky Companion, but letting an agent use them may be against their terms. Apps can also see that USB debugging or Wireless debugging is on, which Pinky needs on every Android phone; some apps, banking apps among them, warn you or refuse to run while it is. It stays on for as long as you use the phone with Pinky. So Pinky turns the service on only while an agent works on the phone: as a task starts, and off again a few seconds after the task ends or you take over the phone, or a minute after the agent's last step. The rest of the time it is off, and those apps work as usual. While an agent works, even on the phone's background display, they see it: to use one of them then, click **Take over** in Pinky first, or end the task. To keep Pinky from turning the service on at all, uninstall Pinky Companion on the phone (Android's Settings › Apps). Pinky works without it, only more slowly: it reads a screen in about 2 s instead of 70 ms, and types text other than plain English through the phone's clipboard. **Not now** on the phone's page puts away Pinky's offer to install it again.
How is Pinky different from other phone tools for agents? We looked at more than a dozen before building it. None of the open-source ones covers iPhone and Android, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, works with any agent and keeps a person in the loop, all at once. Most leave it to the agent to ask first, or block whole kinds of actions; Pinky holds the one risky tap itself, outside the agent, and records every run.
Is it safe to give my phone to an agent that can run commands? An agent that can run commands as you could reach the phone without Pinky, through adb for example, and skip its rules. Run such agents in a sandbox without access to the phone, or plug the phone into another computer and let the agent connect to Pinky there over HTTP ([how](docs/mcp.md#over-http)).
## Build from source To use Pinky, install a release ([Get started](#get-started)). Building it yourself, to work on it, needs Go 1.27.3 or later, and on a Mac Xcode's command line tools. Pinky is one Go binary without cgo; MyGo (`go tool mygo build`) packages it for each system. The live mirror and recordings use FFmpeg 9's shared libraries, which Pinky loads at run time: from `PINKY_FFMPEG_DIR`, from the app (macOS), next to the executable, then from where the system keeps libraries. Every release carries its own minimal LGPL build (`scripts/ffmpeg.sh`, the H.264 and HEVC decoders): in Pinky.app, and next to the executable in the Windows installer and zip and in the Linux `.tar.gz` and `.deb` ([docs/RELEASING.md](docs/RELEASING.md#ffmpeg)). A build of your own needs one too: `make app` adds it to Pinky.app, and `scripts/release.sh build` makes every package with it. Without FFmpeg everything but the mirror works, and Pinky says what is missing. ### macOS ```sh make companion # optional: the Android companion APK (Android SDK and JDK) make app # build/pinky/darwin-/Pinky.app and pinky--.dmg ``` `make app` builds a minimal LGPL FFmpeg 9 from source the first time (`make ffmpeg`, about a minute: the H.264 and HEVC decoders with VideoToolbox), puts it in `Pinky.app/Contents/Frameworks`, with CMake installed (`brew install cmake`) also builds Pinky's own adb (`make adb`) into `Contents/Helpers`, adds the companion APK when it is built (`COMPANION_APK=path` picks another), signs the app and makes the `.dmg` from the finished app. Install from the `.dmg` by dragging Pinky to Applications. The app is signed ad hoc unless `macos.signingIdentity` in `cmd/pinky/mygo.json` (or `make app MACOS_SIGN=…`) names a Developer ID; an ad-hoc signed app runs on the Mac that built it, and another Mac's Gatekeeper refuses it. `make app` does not notarize. `make release` signs with the Developer ID in `RELEASE_SIGN` and notarizes the `.dmg` (`make notarize`: submit, wait, staple), with the notarytool profile in `NOTARY_PROFILE` (`pinky-notary`), which you store once with `xcrun notarytool store-credentials pinky-notary --apple-id --team-id `. Releases themselves are built, signed and published by a workflow for both kinds of Mac, Windows and Linux; see [docs/RELEASING.md](docs/RELEASING.md). To try your build, open it (`open build/pinky/darwin-arm64/Pinky.app`) and connect your agent to it with Connect in its Settings › Agents, which uses this build's path, or for Claude Code from the checkout: ```sh claude mcp add --scope user pinky -- "$PWD/build/pinky/darwin-arm64/Pinky.app/Contents/MacOS/Pinky" mcp mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/pinky && cp docs/SKILL.md ~/.claude/skills/pinky/SKILL.md ``` `go run ./cmd/pinky` does not see the app's FFmpeg: install FFmpeg 9 with Homebrew (`brew install ffmpeg`) or point at the build, `PINKY_FFMPEG_DIR=build/ffmpeg/lib go run ./cmd/pinky`. Unlocking a phone from the computer keeps its PIN in the login keychain and asks for Touch ID or the Mac's password each time. ### Windows ```sh go tool mygo build -platform windows/amd64 cmd/pinky # build/pinky/windows-amd64/Pinky.exe (and an installer where NSIS is installed) go build -o pinky.exe ./cmd/pinky # a console build, for pinky devices and other commands in a terminal ``` Pinky.exe is a windowed program: agents that start `Pinky.exe mcp` talk to it over pipes, but a terminal shows nothing it prints, so use the console build there. A release's installer and zip carry FFmpeg next to `Pinky.exe` (with D3D11VA). For a build of your own, `scripts/ffmpeg.sh build/ffmpeg-windows windows-amd64` makes the DLLs in `build/ffmpeg-windows/bin` (in a Docker container); put them next to the executable, or set `PINKY_FFMPEG_DIR` to their folder (the `ffmpeg-n9.0-…-win64-lgpl-shared` builds at [FFmpeg-Builds](https://github.com/FFmpeg-Builds/FFmpeg-Builds/releases) work too). A build of your own carries no adb, so Android phones need the one of Android's platform tools; `scripts/adb.sh build/adb-windows windows-amd64` builds Pinky's own (in a Docker container), whose `adb.exe` and two DLLs go next to the executable. iPhones are untested on Windows. PINs are kept in the Credential Manager, and each unlock asks through Windows Hello, or for the account's password where Hello is not set up. ### Linux ```sh go tool mygo build -platform linux/amd64 cmd/pinky # build/pinky/linux-amd64/: pinky, a .deb, a .tar.gz with install.sh, a PKGBUILD ``` The window needs GTK 3 and EGL (`libgtk-3-0`, `libegl1`; Mesa draws it in software where there is no GPU). A release's `.tar.gz` and `.deb` carry FFmpeg next to `pinky`; it needs glibc 2.29 or later (Ubuntu 20.04, Debian 11 and newer) and decodes in software. For a build of your own, `scripts/ffmpeg.sh build/ffmpeg-linux linux-amd64` makes the libraries in `build/ffmpeg-linux/lib` (in a Docker container); put them next to the executable, or set `PINKY_FFMPEG_DIR` to their folder. For hardware decoding (VA-API), point `PINKY_FFMPEG_DIR` at an FFmpeg 9 that has it, such as the distribution's or FFmpeg-Builds' shared builds (which need `libva2` and `libva-drm2`); Pinky looks there first. iPhones are untested on Linux. PINs are kept in the Secret Service (GNOME Keyring, KWallet, KeePassXC) in a keyring of Pinky's own, which the first save asks you to give a password and which Pinky locks again after each use, so every unlock asks for that password. ## Build and test ```sh make check # build (CGO_ENABLED=0), vet, test make app # Pinky.app with FFmpeg and the companion, and a .dmg (macOS) make ffmpeg # FFmpeg 9 for Pinky.app, in build/ffmpeg make adb # Pinky's own adb for Pinky.app, in build/adb (needs CMake) make companion # the Android companion APK (Android SDK and JDK needed) make e2e # a binary with MyGo's automation socket, for UI checks scripts/smoke.sh # the fake gateway, pinky devices and a task through pinky mcp make dist # a dry run of a release, in dist// (docs/RELEASING.md) ``` `go run ./cmd/pinky --fake` runs the app with two scripted phones (a payment to approve, a blocked banking app, a password field), so it needs no phone. Tests that need a real phone use the `device` build tag; see [docs/WORKING.md](docs/WORKING.md). `go run ./scripts/secretcheck` checks by hand that unlocking asks you (Touch ID, Windows Hello). `PINKY_FFMPEG_APP=build/pinky/darwin-arm64/Pinky.app go test -run TestPackagedFFmpeg ./internal/video/` checks that the app decodes with its own FFmpeg; given the folder of an unpacked Windows or Linux package, it checks that package's. CI ([.github/workflows/ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml)) builds, vets and tests on Linux and Windows, builds and vets on macOS, runs `scripts/smoke.sh` on all three, packages for Linux and Windows, and on Linux opens the window under Xvfb and captures it through the automation socket. It runs for `main`, pull requests, by hand, and the platform session's `claude/platform-*` branches. ## Code layout ```text cmd/pinky/ app, daemon and MCP shim in one binary internal/screen/ the screen format agents read internal/driver/ driver interfaces; android/ and ios/ implement them internal/gateway/ sessions, leases, the action pipeline, the client API internal/policy/, approval/ rules and approvals internal/history/ task history (SQLite) internal/mcp/ the MCP server internal/api/ the local socket for agents and clients internal/demo/ scripted fake phones internal/update/ new versions: the feed, checks, the swap, What's new internal/video/, ui/ the desktop client (MyGo native UI, FFmpeg decoding) internal/telemetry/ usage statistics, crash reports and feedback worker/ the Cloudflare Worker that receives usage statistics and crash reports android/companion/ the Android companion app (Kotlin) scripts/ device locks and an MCP call script for checks docs/ design, agent guide, MCP reference and notes ``` ## Documents - [Acceptance checklist](docs/ACCEPTANCE.md) - [Design](docs/DESIGN.md) - [Agent guide (SKILL.md)](docs/SKILL.md) and [MCP reference](docs/mcp.md) - [Phones away from home](docs/away-from-home.md) - [Working on Pinky](docs/WORKING.md) - [Usage statistics, crash reports and feedback](docs/TELEMETRY.md) - Notes: [integration](docs/notes/integration.md), [gateway](docs/notes/gateway.md), [Android](docs/notes/android.md), [companion](docs/notes/companion.md), [iOS](docs/notes/ios.md), [client](docs/notes/client.md), [updates](docs/notes/updates.md), [telemetry](docs/notes/telemetry.md), [app logs](docs/notes/app-logs.md) - [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) ## Community Ask questions, share what your agent does on your phone and follow development on [Discord](https://discord.gg/S27b7SHjng). Bugs and feature requests are welcome as GitHub issues; Help › Send Feedback… in Pinky opens one with diagnostics filled in. ## License Apache-2.0

# Google Pro Helper

本仓库收录两个独立版本：浏览器扩展版与批量版，分别保留各自的目录结构和原有代码。

| 版本 | 目录 | 简介 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 浏览器扩展版 | [extension](./extension/) | 在浏览器中使用的扩展项目，包含扩展清单、弹窗页面、脚本与图标。 |
| 批量版 | [batch](./batch/) | 用于批量账号任务管理的本地控制台项目，包含网页界面、后端、启动脚本与测试。 |

google-pro-helper/
├── extension/   # 浏览器扩展版

## 批量版

**Google AI Pro (5 TB) 零成本两年 (US$0.00 -> 24个月) 全自动控制台**

> 以上述“零成本两年”为项目目标，不代表已验证的订阅结果。原说明中的“全程 0 扣费”不能作为保证，实际费用和权益以结账页面及上游结果为准。

### 一、运行环境要求
1. Windows 10 / 11 系统
2. 已安装 Google Chrome 浏览器（默认路径即可）
3. 已安装 Python 3.10 或更高版本（安装时勾选 Add Python to PATH）
4. 网络环境：本机开启美区（US）代理，或在控制台左侧填写代理模板

### 二、快速启动步骤
1. 首次使用请双击运行：【1_首次运行_安装依赖并启动.bat】
2. 之后日常使用直接双击：【2_启动控制台.bat】
3. 浏览器会自动打开控制台页面：http://127.0.0.1:8765

### 三、自定义填写支付卡 & 跑号说明
#### 1. 填写支付卡（必填）：
   - 在网页左侧【全局配置与内联免税绑卡】区域，填入你自己的 Visa 或 Mastercard 外币卡：
     * 卡号（16位数字）
     * 有效期（月 / 年，如 08 / 29）
     * 安全码（3位 CVC）
     * 持卡人英文姓名
     * 免税邮编默认已填好 97201（美国俄勒冈免税州），无需修改
   - 填写后点击【💾 保存配置】。
   - 注：脚本内置严格 0 元消费保护，仅在结账弹窗确认为 US$0.00 时才会点击订阅，全程 0 扣费。

#### 2. 批量导入 Google 账号：
   - 在网页右侧【批量放号导入区】粘贴账号（每行一个），支持以下任意格式：
     * 邮箱----密码----辅助邮箱
     * 邮箱----密码----辅助邮箱----2FA密钥
     * 邮箱----密码----2FA密钥
   - 点击【➕ 一键导入账号列表】。

#### 3. 开始全自动执行：
   - 点击单个账号右侧的【▶ 执行】或顶部的【▶ 批量全自动执行】。
   - 脚本会自动完成：
     - Step 1: 自动登录 Google 并通过辅助邮箱 / 2FA 验证
     - Step 2: 内联免税绑卡 + 首层 12 个月免费包 (US$0.00)
     - Step 3: 叠加二层 6 个月免费包 (US$0.00 -> 18个月)
     - Step 4: 叠加三层 6 个月免费包 (US$0.00 -> 24个月封顶)
     - Step 5: 自动前往 Google Play 取消自动续订，锁死 2 年到期权益并截图验真

### 四、隔离与敏感数据

- 浏览器扩展版位于 `extension/`，批量版位于 `batch/`，两者分目录存放。批量版原启动脚本使用当前 Python 环境安装依赖，未提供独立虚拟环境，不能宣称依赖完全隔离。
- 批量版按账号使用独立浏览器配置目录，但这不等于虚拟机或安全沙箱。
- 账号密码、2FA 密钥、支付卡信息和浏览器登录数据属于敏感信息；本地配置、浏览器配置目录、截图、日志及缓存不应提交到仓库。


## 使用入口

- **浏览器扩展版**：打开 Chrome 扩展管理页，开启开发者模式，选择“加载已解压的扩展程序”，加载 `extension` 目录。
- **批量版**：在 Windows 下进入 `batch` 目录，首次使用运行 `1_首次运行_安装依赖并启动.bat`，之后运行 `2_启动控制台.bat`。

两个版本独立使用。本次整理仅增加仓库分层和本页介绍，不修改项目源代码。

本地账号与支付配置（`config*.json`）、环境变量文件、缓存和运行数据不提交到仓库；批量版的配置请在本地填写。

items.readme:
Erosion-CN

基于 worse_query 的 iOS / iPadOS 系统配置与 MobileGestalt 研究工具箱（简体中文防白苹果安全加固版）

支持 iOS / iPadOS 27.0 – 27.2 / 27.3 beta 1（完整支持）以及 iOS / iPadOS 26.x（部分支持）。

--- ## 项目简介与核心改进 **Erosion-CN** 分支衍生自官方上游项目 **[jailbreakdotparty/Erosion](https://github.com/jailbreakdotparty/Erosion)**，完成了 **100% 简体中文界面本地化**，修复了原版多项严重真机 Bug，并进行了系统级防白苹果安全加固与底层能力扩展： 1. **修复重启后修改自动失效还原（反弹回原厂状态）的严重 Bug** - 原版在未手动切换过设置开关时，`mgWriteAtomically` 默认返回 `false`，导致实际走了临时文件替换（`replaceItemAt`），破坏了系统缓存文件的 Inode 与 `_mobilegestalt` POSIX 属主权限，设备一重启即被系统丢弃重建；同时原版在 iOS 27 上额外注入了非缓存键 `RegionInfo`（`zHeENZu+wbg7PUprwNwBWg`），触发开机缓存合法性校验整包重置。 - 本分支已默认强制锁定原位覆盖写入，严格遵循 iOS 27 原厂缓存键结构，并自动匹配写入对应机型的监管型号（`RegulatoryModelNumber`），**真正做到持久化生效、重启不反弹**。 2. **修复内置 Plist 编辑器破坏布尔值与相机浮点参数导致「相机黑屏」的严重 Bug** - 原版 `PlistManager` 将 `CFBoolean`（`` / ``）以及整数值 `Double`（如相机变焦倍率 `1.0`、`2.0`、`5.0` 等）误判转换为了 `` 整型，导致编辑保存 `MobileGestalt` 后系统相机取景直接黑屏。 - 本分支改用 `CFBooleanGetTypeID()` 与 `CFNumberIsFloatType()` 精确识别底层 CoreFoundation 类型，保留原始 Plist 根类型与编码格式，并对未修改项执行 **100% 原样无损直通（Lossless Pass-through）**，彻底解决相机黑屏问题。 3. **零 0 字节窗口原位写入协议（`pwrite` + 按需尾截断 + `F_FULLFSYNC`）** - 重构底层文件 I/O：不再先执行 `ftruncate(fd, 0)` 清空系统文件，而是直接从偏移 `0` 原位覆盖写入、写完后按需裁剪尾部，并调用 `fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC)` 强制刷新 APFS 与物理闪存缓存，断电或异常中断绝不留空文件。 4. **写入前变更对比预览（Diff Preview）+ 写后全量读回校验与自动回滚** - 点击「应用」时逐条展示所有待修改键值与十六进制槽位对比（`修改前 → 修改后`）； - 写入前自动保存 `PreApplyGestalt.plist` 快照，写入后立即从磁盘读回并做二进制 Plist 反序列化与严格类型校验，一旦出现任何不一致立即自动原位回滚。 5. **本机 `libMobileGestalt.dylib` 运行时动态偏移解析（零硬编码）** - 在设备运行时只读扫描内存中加载的 `/usr/lib/libMobileGestalt.dylib` 查询描述符表，实时计算当前机型与当前系统版本的 `CacheUUID`、总槽位数及布尔槽位偏移（`green-tea`、`not-green-tea`、`wapi`）； - **严格多重校验门控**：仅当本机 `CacheUUID` 唯一匹配、总长度精确等于 `槽位数 × 9`、有效位 `validity == 1`、8 字节槽位填充全为 `0` 且无任何无关字节变动时才允许修改；解析未通过时自动锁定开关并拦截写入。 6. **跨机型 / 跨系统升级四重指纹防呆、SHA-256 备份摘要校验与云备份隔离** - 本地备份文件自动标记 `isExcludedFromBackup = true`，防止通过 iCloud / 电脑换机迁移时将旧设备的缓存备份带入新设备； - 生成原始备份 `OriginalGestalt.plist` 时自动计算并持久化记录 `SHA-256` 完整性摘要；还原原始备份时强制核对 `SHA-256`、`CacheVersion`、`CacheUUID`、`CacheData` 长度与本机硬件 `ProductType`，从根源上杜绝跨系统升级或损坏备份覆写导致的基带/eSIM 异常。 7. **重签证书 `App Group` 自动探测与高危软砖项拆除** - 运行时通过 `SecTaskCopyValueForEntitlement` 与纯 Swift Mach-O `LC_CODE_SIGNATURE` 签名段解析自动匹配任意重签工具注入的可用 `group.*` 容器； - 默认移除并拦截上游版本中存在软砖/无限设置向导隐患的高危功能（如 iPhone 正则盲改切片的 iPadOS 模式、个人零售设备的监管模式开关、非缓存键注入等）。 8. **完善机型适配、iOS 27 进阶 AI 能力解锁与实用工具优化** - 补全 iPhone 15 / 16 / 17 / Air / 18 / Duo 全系列及 M 系列 iPad 监管型号映射与硬件特征表，修复原版“80% 充电上限”与“开机提示音”硬件判断互换笔误及自定义键值恒写入 `true` 的 Bug； - **Apple 智能子能力打包与 iOS 27 进阶 AI 解锁（`v0.6.2`）**：「启用 Apple 智能开关」自动联动解锁旧机型缺失的相册「消除」(Clean Up) 与备忘录「手写体合成」能力；新增 **「解锁 iOS 27 进阶 AI 能力」** 合并开关，支持为 iPhone 15 Pro / 16 / 17 等机型一键解锁默认仅在最新代硬件设备树 (`IODeviceTree:/product`) 中开启的**个人实时翻译 (`Personal Translator`)** 与 **iOS 27 音频智能 (`Audio Intelligence`)**（注：**iPhone 18 系列机型硬件底层已默认开启上述能力，无需额外开启，故应用内默认不展示该选项**，国行设备仅需开启「解除地区限制」即可完整激活）； - 新增 iOS 26/27「液态玻璃低功耗渲染（省电模式）」开关与机型外层描述同步； - 修复文件浏览器搜索栏失效与失焦清空问题，采用 `stat()` 动态探测本机实时最大 Inode 基线配合 `pathleak` 加速容器扫描（并为动态壁纸与拨号盘页面加入异步加载进度动画），同时新增核心缓存目录 0 秒一键直达入口； 9. **新增应用存档管理与容器缓存清理模块（`v0.6.0`）** - **应用与游戏存档备份、还原与修改器 (`AppDataBackupView`)**：自动扫描本机第三方应用与单机游戏容器，支持一键将 `Documents` 与 `Library/Preferences` 打包备份为 `.zip`、导出分享、跨重装自动匹配最新容器 UUID 原位还原存档，并支持一键跳入存档目录调用内置无损 Plist/文本编辑器修改； - **容器级缓存扫描与清理 (`CacheCleanerView`)**：专治 iOS「系统数据（其他）」暴涨，按体积排行展示各应用容器的 `Library/Caches` 与 `tmp` 可释放空间，支持单应用或批量一键清理（严格保护 `Documents`、聊天记录数据库与登录态）。 10. **新增真机底层生效核验探针、Apple 智能四要素一键体检、影像/健康硬件槽位解锁与全链路沙盒审计加固（`v0.7.2`）** - **真机 `MobileGestalt` 底层生效核验与动态槽位实时探针 (`MGInspectorView`)**：纯只读调用系统库 `MGCopyAnswer` 实时读取当前真机生效值，并与 `OriginalGestalt.plist` 原厂备份、当前 `CacheData / CacheExtra` 待写配置进行三源同屏对比；同时提供本机全量 `720+` 个二进制 `CacheData` 槽位的动态解析检索与自由键名实时探针； - **Apple 智能 (Apple Intelligence) 激活四要素一键体检面板 (`AppleIntelligenceCheckupCard`)**：实时聚合核验「销售地区 `LL/LL/A`」、「美版监管型号 `Axxxx`（基于真实主板型号防伪装误判）」、「端侧 AI 芯片准入」及「系统实时生效回读」，并在原生 AI 机型上自动锁定 `InternalInstall` 互斥开关，支持一键自动配齐全部缺失项； - **影像与健康进阶能力解锁（`CacheData` 二进制硬件槽位直写）**：针对 `libMobileGestalt.dylib` 中 `_MGCacheSetValueForKey` 的 `validity` 短路机制（仅写 `CacheExtra` 会被系统直接忽略的硬件设备树属性），通过运行时动态槽位解析直接写入 `CacheData`，新增 **相册与相机「混音 (Audio Mix)」**、**空间音频录制与 FaceTime 空间音频**、**按下快门瞬间抓拍 (Responsive Shutter)** 与 **健康「高血压趋势评估模式」** 4 项开关，并内置本机原生硬件防降级保护锁； - **全链路沙盒逃逸与文件编辑安全加固（`v0.7.2`）**：修复内置 Plist 编辑器因 `@Binding` 原地变异导致保存回旧值的 Bug；重构 `WorseQuerySwift` 支持只读容器令牌保留（`requireWrite: false`），修复 `System` / `AppGroup` 容器浏览、容器排序重复扫描、符号链接类型识别、壁纸与拨号盘父容器授权、存档备份还原 xattr 核验与 Zip Slip 防护等 24 个文件的边界缺陷。 --- ## 系统兼容性 > [!IMPORTANT] > 操作前请务必通过电脑完整备份设备重要数据！修改系统底层配置存在潜在风险，仅供安全研究与学习交流，请仅在本人持有的设备上使用并自行承担风险。 - **iOS / iPadOS 27.0 – 27.2.1**、**27.3 beta 1**（完整支持所有功能，包括 `MobileGestalt` 读取与安全写入） - **iOS / iPadOS 26.0 – 26.7.2**（部分支持：可使用锁屏壁纸、拨号键盘美化、锁屏底部签名文字与部分容器浏览；受底层沙盒限制，iOS 26 不支持写入系统 `MobileGestalt`） --- ## 安装与签名要求 > [!WARNING] > 本项目底层依赖至少一个有效的 `App Group` 容器权限。请使用支持保留或注入 App Group 的个人 Apple ID 自签工具（如 **SideStore / AltStore / Feather / Sideloadly / Impactor / iLoader**）或带 App Group 权限的开发者证书签名安装。 1. 前往 [Releases 页面](https://github.com/Kianuni/Erosion-CN/releases/latest) 下载最新的 `Erosion_v0.7.2_zh-Hans.ipa`。 2. 使用上述签名工具安装至设备；首次运行可在「主页」日志确认已成功识别 `App Group`。 3. 详细使用说明与原厂状态恢复教程请查阅： - 📘 [USAGE_GUIDE.md（安装与使用指南）](./USAGE_GUIDE.md) - 🔄 [RESTORE_CHA.md（无损恢复出厂状态指南）](./RESTORE_CHA.md) --- ## 自行编译 在安装有 Xcode 26 / 27 的 macOS 环境中克隆本仓库并执行构建脚本即可生成未签名 `.ipa`（已自动内嵌标准 entitlements）： ```bash git clone https://github.com/Kianuni/Erosion-CN.git cd Erosion-CN chmod +x ipabuild.sh ./ipabuild.sh ``` --- ## 致谢与开源许可 (Credits & License) 本项目基于 **[GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPLv3)](./LICENSE)** 开源，谨向上游作者与社区研究者致以诚挚感谢： ### 特别致谢（特性借鉴与研究参考） -
